Facts by #JoeHansenFacts Why are Starlink's space lasers such a big deal? Without lasers, a satellite has to send your data straight back down to a ground station it can see. No ground station in range, no internet. Starlink skips that step. 1. Each V2 Mini satellite carries 3 lasers that talk directly to other satellites. 2. More than 24,000 of these lasers are up there now, forming one mesh around the planet. 3. Each link runs at up to 200 Gbps. SpaceX says hardware next year moves that to 400. 4. Data can hop from satellite to satellite until it finds a ground station, even on the other side of an ocean. That's why it works on a cruise ship in the middle of the Pacific, and why it kept working in Spain and Portugal when the whole power grid went down in April 2025. Smarter laser routing also cut 30 to 40 ms of latency in Asia and Africa in 2025.

The sudden collapse of the value of CoT (even summarized CoT) in the agentic era changes working with AI. Effectively steering AIs and getting any sort of observability now requires you to ask for interim outputs & tests, and to use AI help to troubleshoot problems you find.

It used to be that you could look at the CoT from a request and get a sense of where the model was going, but with tons of agents calling other agents, and CoTs that run to thousands of pages for even simple agentic tasks, that is no longer possible.

It also requires you to trust the orchestrator model more than ever, since it is the only thing that can track all of the tasks. Which means you need to use AI to both find problems with AI and to troubleshoot problems you find.

New work from Meta AI on agents that manage their own search. (bookmark it) A ReAct agent keeps every failed attempt in one context, making useful evidence harder to find. To improve on this, they propose TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent’s own policy decides where to search. In TreeFlex, the agent saves each intermediate state as a node in a search tree. The same model then reads short summaries of all nodes and decides where to continue, whether to branch, when to check a proposed answer, and when to stop. On a deep-research benchmark, a 4B model reaches 48.8% versus 41.5% for flat ReAct, at the same context limit. Same 9B base model, both trained with RL. 54.9% on SWE-bench Verified with TreeFlex, versus 43.3% with FoldAgent. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20334 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/treeflex-agents-navigating-their-own-search-trees-2610.20334

Must-read paper from Sakana AI on orchestrating coding agents for scientific research. (bookmark it) This is an important read with lots of useful insights if you are building multi-agent systems. I like this work because it presents a concrete multi-agent framework and an end-to-end distributed pipeline that lets human researchers conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. What they did: A development version of their system helped write a paper that was accepted as a main-conference talk at ALIFE 2026, after human verification and edits. How they did it: The Agentic Scientist splits a project into stages. Task drafting, ideation, planning, sandboxed experiments, baselines and ablations, analysis, and report writing each run on a coding agent that checks its own work. A meta-controller runs many of these agents in parallel and checks every stage against a rubric. The ablations show that reliable autonomy depends on that orchestration layer as well as on the base model. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18933 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/the-agentic-scientist-orchestrating-coding-agents-for-automated-scientific-co-di-2610.18933

Fascinating paper from Google DeepMind. They studied a market where AI agents bid to answer each user prompt. Each agent bids its expected reward minus its inference cost. A first-price auction is simple to run, but bidders shade their bids, so a prompt can go to an agent that would not have produced the most value. The paper shows two features of agent markets that keep this loss small. When several agents value a prompt close to the best one, for example because strong models are distilled into cheaper ones, competition limits the loss. When values mostly depend on how hard the prompt is, efficiency approaches 1 - 1/e^2 of optimal, well above the general bound of 1 - 1/e. They find that simulations on the EmbedLLM routing dataset match the theory. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20587 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/price-of-anarchy-of-first-price-auctions-in-agentic-markets-2610.20587
